scenes.learning_objective: Explain how a learned world model changes the sample-efficiency problem in reinforcement learning.
scenes.summary: The narrator frames model-based reinforcement learning as a bargain: learn a simulator of experience, then use it to choose actions with fewer real trials.
scenes.title: Model Before Policy

scenes.learning_objective: Describe what a latent world model stores and why imagined rollouts are useful for control.
scenes.summary: The scene moves from pixels to compressed states, showing why latent rollouts make imagination cheap enough to train policies inside predicted futures.
scenes.title: Dream Space

scenes.learning_objective: Diagnose why long imagined rollouts can become unreliable even when one-step predictions look accurate.
scenes.summary: The narrator follows a small prediction mistake as it grows over multiple imagined steps, introducing compounding prediction error as the central tax on planning with learned models.
scenes.title: Error Horizon

acts.summary: This act establishes why world models matter: agents learn compact latent futures, then improve behavior inside imagined rollouts instead of only through real interaction.
acts.title: Latent Dreams

scenes.learning_objective: Compare a single-vector latent state with an object-centric representation for multi-object prediction.
scenes.summary: The scene contrasts monolithic latent states with worlds made of reusable parts, making object-centric representation the answer to scaling across different numbers and arrangements of things.
scenes.title: The Combinatorial Wall

scenes.learning_objective: Explain how relational inductive bias helps a model generalize across object configurations.
scenes.summary: The narrator introduces nodes, edges, and shared update rules as a relational inductive bias that lets a model reuse what it learns about one interaction in another scene.
scenes.title: Relational Bias

scenes.learning_objective: Predict the role of message passing in an action-conditioned graph dynamics model.
scenes.summary: The scene treats message passing as learned local physics: objects send influence along edges, aggregate effects, and update their future states under an action-conditioned graph dynamics model.
scenes.title: Messages As Physics

scenes.learning_objective: Explain why permutation equivariance is required for object-centric graph world models.
scenes.summary: The narrator explains permutation equivariance through reordered objects: the graph model should change labels consistently, not change the physical prediction.
scenes.title: Order Does Not Matter

acts.summary: This act shows why graphs enter the story: multi-object worlds explode combinatorially unless the model represents entities, relations, and repeatable interaction rules.
acts.title: Objects And Relations

scenes.learning_objective: Describe how slot attention plus latent GNN dynamics can build an object-centric world model from observations.
scenes.summary: The scene links slot attention and latent GNNs, showing how a model can first separate entities from observations and then simulate their interactions.
scenes.title: Learning The Slots

scenes.learning_objective: Choose between reconstruction and contrastive objectives for a given graph world-model training goal.
scenes.summary: The narrator compares reconstruction losses with contrastive objectives, emphasizing that the training signal shapes whether the latent graph preserves pixels, controllable structure, or task-relevant distinctions.
scenes.title: What To Train For

scenes.learning_objective: Explain how MPC or MCTS can use graph latent rollouts to choose an action.
scenes.summary: The scene shows MPC, heuristic search, and MCTS rolling actions forward over graph latents, selecting actions by evaluating predicted futures without committing to a full policy first.
scenes.title: Search In The Graph

scenes.learning_objective: Synthesize the three roles of graphs in world models and identify the tradeoff each role introduces.
scenes.summary: The final scene summarizes the graph as three roles at once: connector between entities, simulator of dynamics, and reasoner for planning across possible futures.
scenes.title: Connector Simulator Reasoner

acts.summary: This act connects representation to action: graph latents become simulators for MPC, search, and MCTS, while training objectives decide what structure the model actually learns.
acts.title: Planning Over Graphs

discovery_seed_plan.brief: Use Ha and Schmidhuber's 2018 World Models as the cinematic origin point for agents trained inside learned latent dreams.
discovery_seed_plan.deep: Tie the paper to the idea that a compact latent simulator can support policy learning without constant real-environment interaction.

discovery_seed_plan.brief: Use Battaglia's Interaction Networks and later Graph Networks work as the bridge from object relations to learned physical simulation.
discovery_seed_plan.deep: The historical hook is that message passing looked like differentiable physics before it became a world-model planning substrate.

discovery_seed_plan.brief: Use Kipf's Contrastive Structured World Models to motivate why learning object-centric graph latents is not just a reconstruction problem.
discovery_seed_plan.deep: Contrast reconstruction-heavy latent dreams with objectives that preserve controllable distinctions and relational structure.

discovery_seed_plan.brief: Use Hafner's Dreamer line as the practical proof that latent imagination can drive high-performing model-based control.
discovery_seed_plan.deep: Position Dreamer as the workhorse baseline before asking what changes when the latent state becomes explicitly object-centric and graph-structured.

discovery_seed_plan.brief: Use recent graph world-model and object-centric MCTS papers to stage the return of planning over learned structured states.
discovery_seed_plan.deep: The later lesson can contrast short-horizon MPC, heuristic search, and tree search under model error and branching-factor pressure.

notes: No interactive components were supplied, so all scenes are narration-first and leave room for later shot design, diagrams, and optional simulations.
